testName: IISER IAT - Structural Organisation in Plants and Animals (20 Questions)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a typical dicot root, which tissue constitutes the bulk of the central region and serves as the primary site for storage of food reserves?
options: Epidermis with root hairs
Cortex consisting of parenchyma cells
Endodermis with Casparian strips
Pith composed of parenchyma
questions.explanation:
Step 1: In dicot roots, the vascular tissue forms a solid core in the center (xylem and phloem alternate).
Step 2: The cortex, located between epidermis and endodermis, consists of several layers of parenchyma cells that make up the bulk of the root and serve as the primary storage tissue for starch and other food reserves.
Step 3: The pith in dicot roots is either very small or absent (unlike monocot roots where pith is prominent).
Why others are wrong: (A) Epidermis is protective, not storage; (C) Endodermis is regulatory (Casparian strips control water/mineral entry); (D) Pith is negligible in dicot roots.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The arrangement of vascular bundles in the stem of a typical dicotyledonous plant is best described as:
options: Scattered throughout the ground tissue without any definite pattern
Arranged in a ring forming a eustele with distinct cambium
Located only in the center of the stem as a solid core
Absent, with vascular tissue forming a continuous cylinder
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Dicot stems exhibit eustele - a type of stele where vascular bundles are arranged in a ring or circle around the periphery of the pith.
Step 2: This arrangement features:
• Conjoint collateral open bundles (xylem inner, phloem outer, with cambium between)
• Ring of vascular bundles with pith in center and cortex outside
• This allows for secondary growth (increase in girth)
Why others are wrong: (A) Scattered bundles describe monocot stems (atactostele); (C) Solid core describes dicot roots, not stems; (D) Vascular bundles are distinct, not a continuous cylinder.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the leaf anatomy of C4 plants (like maize) compared to C3 plants is CORRECT?
options: C4 plants lack bundle sheath cells and have only mesophyll cells performing photosynthesis
C4 plants have Kranz anatomy with two distinct types of photosynthetic cells: mesophyll and bundle sheath cells
C4 plants have their vascular bundles scattered similar to their stem anatomy
C4 plants lack stomata on the upper epidermis and only have them on the lower epidermis
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Kranz anatomy (German for 'wreath') is the defining leaf feature of C4 plants.
Step 2: It consists of:
• Mesophyll cells - peripheral, perform initial CO₂ fixation using PEP carboxylase
• Bundle sheath cells - arranged in a wreath around vascular bundles, thick-walled, large chloroplasts, perform Calvin cycle
• This spatial separation minimizes photorespiration
Why others are wrong: (A) C4 plants HAVE bundle sheath cells - this is essential to C4 pathway; (C) Bundle arrangement in leaves follows venation pattern, not stem pattern; (D) C4 plants often have stomata on both surfaces (isobilateral leaves).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the semi-technical description of a flowering plant (following Bentham and Hooker system), which of the following represents the correct sequence for describing floral characteristics?
options: Calyx → Corolla → Androecium → Gynoecium → Placentation
Corolla → Calyx → Androecium → Gynoecium → Fruit type
Androecium → Gynoecium → Calyx → Corolla → Inflorescence
Inflorescence → Calyx → Corolla → Gynoecium → Androecium
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Standard format for floral description (Bentham & Hooker system):
1. Bracts and Bracteoles (if present)
2. Calyx (sepals) - number, fusion, aestivation
3. Corolla (petals) - number, fusion, aestivation
4. Androecium (stamens) - number, fusion, attachment, dehiscence
5. Gynoecium (carpels) - number, fusion, ovary position, placentation
6. Fruit and Seed
Step 2: The sequence follows the ascending order of floral whorls from outer to inner.
Why others are wrong: (B) Calyx comes before corolla (outer to inner); (C) Androecium and gynoecium are inner whorls, described after outer whorls; (D) Inflorescence is described before flower, but gynoecium comes after androecium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A floral formula shows: ⊕, ⚲, K(₅), C₁₊₂+(₂), A₍₉₎₊₁, G₁. Which family does this flower belong to and what type of aestivation does the corolla show?
options: Solanaceae with valvate aestivation
Fabaceae with vexillary (papilionaceous) aestivation
Liliaceae with twisted aestivation
Brassicaceae with valvate aestivation
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Decode the floral formula:
• ⊕ = Actinomorphic (actually zygomorphic in this case, standard symbol)
• ⚲ = Bisexual
• K(₅) = 5 sepals, united
• C₁₊₂+(₂) = 5 petals: 1 standard (posterior), 2 wings (lateral), 2 fused keel (anterior) - papilionaceous corolla
• A₍₉₎₊₁ = 10 stamens, diadelphous (9 fused + 1 free)
• G₁ = Monocarpellary, superior ovary
Step 2: These are diagnostic features of Fabaceae (Leguminosae).
Step 3: The corolla shows vexillary aestivation (standard outside, wings, keel inside).
Why others are wrong: (A) Solanaceae have 5 fused petals, actinomorphic; (C) Liliaceae have 6 tepals, no such differentiation; (D) Brassicaceae have 4 petals in cross (cruciform).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the family Solanaceae but NOT found in family Liliaceae?
options: Superior ovary and axile placentation
Trimerous flower and superior ovary
Bicarpellary syncarpous ovary and axile placentation
Six stamens and trilocular ovary
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Compare key features:
Solanaceae (e.g., tomato, potato, petunia):
• Bicarpellary (2 carpels), syncarpous
• Axile placentation
• 5 fused petals
• Oblique ovary (tilted)
Liliaceae (e.g., lily, onion, tulip):
• Tricarpellary (3 carpels), syncarpous
• Axile placentation
• 6 tepals (undifferentiated petals/sepals)
• Superior ovary
Step 2: Bicarpellary syncarpous ovary is unique to Solanaceae among these options.
Why others are wrong: (A) Both have superior ovary and axile placentation; (B) Trimerous is Liliaceae, not Solanaceae; (D) Six stamens is Liliaceae (trimerous), Solanaceae typically has 5.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a typical dicot leaf, the vascular bundle (vein) is surrounded by a layer of parenchymatous cells called bundle sheath. In C3 plants, what is the primary function of these cells?
options: To perform the initial fixation of CO₂ using PEP carboxylase
To provide structural support to the leaf lamina
To act as a reservoir for storing water and minerals
To regenerate RuBP for the Calvin cycle
questions.explanation:
Step 1: In C3 plants (like rice, wheat, spinach), the bundle sheath cells are typically:
• Parenchymatous (thin-walled)
• Not specialized for photosynthesis like in C4 plants
• Primary function is structural support and conduction
Step 2: Unlike C4 plants where bundle sheath cells are the site of Calvin cycle, in C3 plants all photosynthesis occurs in mesophyll cells.
Why others are wrong: (A) PEP carboxylase is C4 mesophyll enzyme; (C) Bundle sheath is not primarily for storage; (D) RuBP regeneration occurs in mesophyll chloroplasts in C3 plants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The ground tissue system in a dicot stem consists of:
options: Only pith in the center
Cortex, endodermis, pericycle, pith rays, and pith
Only cortex and pith without any distinct layers
Epidermis, cortex, and vascular bundles only
questions.explanation:
Step 1: The ground tissue system (fundamental tissue) includes all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles.
Step 2: In dicot stem, it comprises:
• Cortex - hypodermis (often collenchyma) + general cortex (parenchyma)
• Endodermis - starch sheath (stores starch)
• Pericycle - often parenchymatous, may contain resin canals
• Pith rays (medullary rays) - between vascular bundles
• Pith - central portion
Why others are wrong: (A) Too limited - ignores cortex and other layers; (C) There are distinct layers; (D) Epidermis is dermal tissue, not ground tissue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the secondary growth in dicot stems is INCORRECT?
options: Secondary growth is initiated by the activity of vascular cambium and cork cambium
Vascular cambium cuts off secondary xylem towards the outside and secondary phloem towards the inside
Cork cambium (phellogen) produces cork (phellem) towards the outside and secondary cortex (phelloderm) towards the inside
Annual rings in wood are formed due to seasonal variations in the activity of vascular cambium
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze secondary growth process:
• Vascular cambium is a meristematic layer between primary xylem and primary phloem
• It divides periclinally (tangentially)
• Secondary xylem (wood) is produced towards the inside (center)
• Secondary phloem is produced towards the outside (periphery)
Step 2: Statement B is INCORRECT - it reverses the positions of secondary xylem and phloem.
Why others are correct: (A) Both cambia are responsible for secondary growth; (C) Correct description of phellogen activity; (D) Spring wood (earlywood) and autumn wood (latewood) form annual rings.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the anatomy of a monocot root (e.g., maize), which of the following is a distinguishing feature compared to a dicot root?
options: Presence of a well-developed pith in the center composed of parenchyma
Absence of pericycle layer outside the vascular bundles
Presence of tetrarch or polyarch xylem arrangement
Absence of endodermis with Casparian strips
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Key differences between monocot and dicot roots:
Monocot root:
• Well-developed pith in center (parenchyma)
• Polyarch (many xylem bundles, usually more than 6)
• Vascular bundles alternate with pith rays
Dicot root:
• No pith or very small pith - solid xylem core in center
• Diarch to tetrarch (2-4 xylem bundles)
• Xylem forms solid core
Step 2: Prominent pith is the distinguishing feature of monocot roots.
Why others are wrong: (B) Both have pericycle; (C) Polyarch is monocot, but this describes xylem arrangement, not the most obvious difference; (D) Both have endodermis with Casparian strips.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The fruit of mango (Mangifera indica) is classified as a drupe. Which statement correctly describes its structure?
options: Entirely fleshy fruit derived from superior ovary with seeds scattered in the pulp
Fleshy fruit with stony endocarp surrounding a single seed, derived from monocarpellary superior ovary
Dry dehiscent fruit splitting along two sutures with multiple seeds attached to marginal placenta
Fleshy fruit with papery endocarp and multiple seeds covered by fleshy thalamus
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Drupe (stone fruit) characteristics:
• Simple fleshy fruit derived from monocarpellary, superior ovary
• Pericarp differentiated into:
- Exocarp - thin skin
- Mesocarp - fleshy, edible portion
- Endocarp - hard, stony layer (pit/stone)
• Contains single seed enclosed in stony endocarp
Step 2: Mango, coconut, peach, plum are typical drupes.
Why others are wrong: (A) Describes berry (e.g., tomato) with multiple seeds; (C) Describes legume (pod) - dry dehiscent; (D) Describes pome (e.g., apple) where fleshy part is thalamus, not ovary wall.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a typical dicot seed (e.g., bean), the embryo consists of two cotyledons and an embryonic axis. The embryonic axis includes:
options: Only the radicle which develops into the root system
The radicle, plumule, and hypocotyl
Only the plumule which develops into the shoot system
The cotyledons and the endosperm
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Dicot seed structure (exalbuminous/endospermic):
• Seed coat (testa + tegmen)
• Cotyledons (2 in dicots) - store food, fleshy
• Embryonic axis:
- Radicle - embryonic root (develops into root system)
- Plumule - embryonic shoot (develops into stem and leaves)
- Hypocotyl - region below cotyledons, above radicle
- Epicotyl - region above cotyledons, below plumule
Step 2: The embryonic axis includes radicle, plumule, and hypocotyl (and epicotyl).
Why others are wrong: (A) Incomplete - misses plumule and hypocotyl; (C) Incomplete - misses radicle and hypocotyl; (D) Cotyledons are separate from axis; endosperm is absent in non-endospermic dicot seeds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the meristematic tissue in plants is CORRECT?
options: Apical meristems are responsible for secondary growth in dicot stems and roots
Intercalary meristems are found at the base of internodes and nodes in grasses and contribute to primary growth
Lateral meristems (vascular cambium and cork cambium) are present in all plant organs including leaves and flowers
Meristematic cells are highly vacuolated with thick cell walls and dense cytoplasm
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Types of meristems:
• Apical meristem - at root and shoot tips, responsible for primary growth (length)
• Intercalary meristem - at base of internodes and nodes (especially in grasses), responsible for elongation of internodes, primary growth
• Lateral meristem (vascular cambium, cork cambium) - responsible for secondary growth (girth), found in stems and roots that undergo secondary growth
Step 2: Intercalary meristems in grasses allow rapid regrowth after grazing.
Why others are wrong: (A) Apical meristems cause primary growth, not secondary; (C) Lateral meristems are NOT in leaves and flowers; (D) Meristematic cells have thin walls, dense cytoplasm, and are non-vacuolated or have small vacuoles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the digestive system of frog (Rana tigrina), the cloaca receives products from:
options: Only the digestive system (intestine)
Digestive system, excretory system, and reproductive system
Only the digestive and excretory systems
Only the excretory and reproductive systems
questions.explanation:
Step 1: The cloaca is a common chamber in frogs (amphibians) that receives:
• Digestive wastes - from rectum (large intestine)
• Excretory wastes - from ureters (urinary bladder opens into cloaca)
• Reproductive products - from oviducts (female) or vas deferens (male)
• Urinary bladder - also opens into cloaca
Step 2: The cloaca is a common exit chamber for digestive, excretory, and reproductive systems in frogs.
Why others are wrong: (A) Too limited - ignores excretory and reproductive; (C) Misses reproductive system; (D) Misses digestive system.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The heart of frog is three-chambered with two atria and one ventricle. Which statement correctly describes the blood flow and oxygenation pattern?
options: Complete separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood with no mixing in the ventricle
Partial mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the ventricle, resulting in incomplete double circulation
Only deoxygenated blood is pumped to all body parts including the lungs
Only oxygenated blood is pumped to all body parts including the body tissues
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog heart structure and function:
• Right atrium - receives deoxygenated blood from body (sinus venosus)
• Left atrium - receives oxygenated blood from lungs and skin
• Single ventricle - receives blood from both atria
• Conus arteriosus - gives rise to truncus arteriosus with three branches
Step 2: In the ventricle, there is partial mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood due to single ventricle.
Step 3: This results in incomplete double circulation - blood goes to lungs/skin and body in a mixed state, less efficient than complete double circulation in birds and mammals.
Why others are wrong: (A) No complete separation - single ventricle causes mixing; (C) Both types of blood are pumped; (D) Both types are pumped, not just oxygenated.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the respiratory system of frog (Rana tigrina)?
options: Only pulmonary respiration through well-developed lungs throughout its life
Cutaneous respiration (through skin) is significant both in water and on land, supplemented by buccal pumping and lungs
Gills are retained throughout adult life for aquatic respiration
Tracheal system with spiracles like in insects
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog respiratory adaptations (amphibian - dual life):
• Cutaneous respiration - through moist, vascular skin (major in water and moist conditions)
• Buccal pumping - force air into lungs by raising and lowering floor of mouth
• Pulmonary respiration - through simple sac-like lungs (less efficient than mammals)
• Buccopharyngeal respiration - through lining of mouth
Step 2: Skin is major respiratory organ; lungs are simple and supplementary.
Why others are wrong: (A) Lungs are poorly developed, not sole respiratory organ; (C) Gills are lost in adult frog (tadpole has gills); (D) Tracheal system is insect feature, not chordate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the male reproductive system of frog, the urine and sperm pass through a common duct called:
options: Ureter
Vas deferens
Urinogenital duct
Oviduct
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Male frog reproductive anatomy:
• Testes - paired, attached to kidneys
• Vasa efferentia - 10-12 ducts from testes enter kidneys
• Bidder's canal - within kidney
• Urinogenital duct - common duct for both urine (from kidney) and sperm (from testes via vasa efferentia)
• Opens into cloaca
Step 2: The urinogenital duct serves as the common passage for excretory and reproductive products in male frogs.
Why others are wrong: (A) Ureter carries only urine in female, but in male it's part of urinogenital system; (B) Vas deferens is specific term in mammals, not used for frog; (D) Oviduct is female reproductive structure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The nervous system of frog consists of central, peripheral, and autonomic nervous systems. Which statement is INCORRECT?
options: The brain is divided into forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain with 10 pairs of cranial nerves
The spinal cord extends throughout the vertebral column and gives rise to 10 pairs of spinal nerves
The autonomic nervous system includes sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
The peripheral nervous system consists of cranial nerves and spinal nerves only
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog nervous system:
• Central Nervous System - brain (10 pairs cranial nerves) + spinal cord
• Peripheral Nervous System - cranial nerves + spinal nerves + autonomic ganglia and nerves
• Autonomic Nervous System - sympathetic (dorsal) and parasympathetic (lateral) chains with ganglia
Step 2: Statement B is INCORRECT - frog has 10 pairs of cranial nerves but 10 pairs of spinal nerves (some sources say 9 or 10), but the error is that spinal cord doesn't extend throughout entire column in adult due to shortening.
Actually, the main error is: Frog has 10 pairs of cranial nerves and 10 pairs of spinal nerves, but spinal cord is short and doesn't fill entire vertebral canal.
Why others are correct: (A) Brain divisions and 10 cranial nerves correct; (C) ANS has both divisions; (D) PNS includes all nerves outside CNS.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the skeletal system of frog?
options: Presence of ribs and sternum for protection of thoracic organs
Absence of tail vertebrae (urostyle is present as a long rod-like structure)
Presence of a well-developed bony tail for swimming
Forelimbs have five digits while hindlimbs have four digits
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog skeletal adaptations (amphibian):
• Vertebral column: 9 presacral vertebrae + 1 sacral + urostyle (elongated, rod-like structure formed by fusion of caudal vertebrae, no free tail)
• No ribs or sternum - doesn't protect thoracic organs with bony cage
• Girdles: Pectoral and pelvic (ilium, ischium, pubis fused to form acetabulum)
• Limbs: Forelimbs (4 digits) and hindlimbs (5 digits, webbed for swimming)
Step 2: Urostyle is a distinctive feature - long, rod-like, no free tail in adult.
Why others are wrong: (A) No ribs or sternum in frog; (C) No bony tail - urostyle replaces tail; (D) Forelimbs have 4 digits, hindlimbs have 5 digits (reversed in statement).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The excretory system of frog includes kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and cloaca. Which statement about frog excretion is CORRECT?
options: Frogs are ureotelic and excrete primarily urea as nitrogenous waste in all life stages and conditions
Frogs are ammonotelic in aquatic conditions (tadpoles) and ureotelic in terrestrial conditions (adults)
Frogs excrete only uric acid as a water-conservation mechanism like reptiles and birds
Frogs lack urinary bladder and excrete urine directly through ureters to the exterior
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog excretory adaptations:
• Tadpoles (aquatic larvae): Ammonotelic - excrete ammonia (NH₃), highly toxic, requires much water for dilution, suitable for aquatic life
• Adults (terrestrial/aquatic): Ureotelic - excrete urea, less toxic, can be stored in urinary bladder, requires less water
• This change is called ureotelic shift during metamorphosis
Step 2: Frogs show ammoniotely in tadpoles and ureotely in adults.
Why others are wrong: (A) Adults are ureotelic, but tadpoles are ammonotelic; (C) Uricotelic is reptile/bird trait, not frog; (D) Frogs HAVE urinary bladder - stores urine before excretion.
